The law provides: "That no part of this appropriation, or any other appropriation provided for herein except appropriations made pursuant to treaties, shall be used to educate children of less than one-fourth Indian blood whose parents are citizens of the United States and of the State wherein they live and where there are adequate free-school facilities provided and the facilities of the Indian schools are needed for pupils of more than one-fourth Indian blood." EXTRACTS FROM SCHOOL RULES. If the facilities of a school are not needed as provided in the above paragraph, children showing any Indian blood, whose parents live on an Indian reservation, and who if debarred from Government schools could not obtain an education, may be enrolled in the day and boarding schools of their reservation; children, however, may not be transferred to nonreservation schools without special permission of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. Before enrolling a pupil superintendents must satisfy themselves whether he has left any other school without permission and whether he has been expelled for cause from any other school. A pupil who has been expelled for cause from any Indian school may be reenrolled in any Indian school only with permission of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. Attention is invited to Circulars Nos. 1039 and 1044, which must be observed. "The Secretary of the Interior may in his discretion withhold rations, clothing, and other annuities from Indian parents or guardians who refuse or neglect to send or keep their children of proper school age in some school during a reasonable portion of each year." (27 Stat. L., 635. See 2 Dec. Comp., 308.) NAME: George Ford Lander Sex: Male. Discharged Dec 30th 1919 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash., Jan. 2, 1920. Mr. E. H. Hammond, Supt., Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Mr. Hammond: Mrs. Antoine Francis is again worrying about the health of her children. Perhaps you recall her visit to your school last year. Someone has recently written her that George Friedlander, her son, was in the hospital and was about to have an operation for the removal of his tonsils. Of course Mrs. Francis objects to this. Will you please write me at your earliest convenience as to George's physical condition? Peter Moses, it is reported, will return to your school sometime between the 5th and 7th of this month. Yours very truly, Fred C. Morgan Superintendent FCM:MG Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Jan. 7, 1920 Dear Mrs. Culbertson: It appears that the mother of George Friedlander is worried over the report that he is about to have an operation for the removal of his tonsils. Please advise me as to his physical condition. Very respectfully, Special Agent in Charge. OHK:MG Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Jan. 12, 1920 Fred C. Morgan, Supt. Colville Indian Agency Roosevelt, Wash. Dear Sir: Relative to the physical condition of George Friedlander you are advised that he entered the hospital on December 8, 1919 with tonsillitis. His tonsils were very much inflamed with ulcers on them. The physician stated that if quinsy developed they would probably have to be lanced. He has fully recovered and left the hospital on December 28, 1919. Very respectfully, Special Agent in Charge. OHK:MG Dear Mr. Peel, Dr. Kemisar asks me to say George Friedlander entered Hospital Dec. 8 - 1919 with Tonsillitis, Tonsils very much inflamed and small ulcers on them. He said if Quinsy developed they would possibly have to be lanced. He has fully recovered and left Hospital Dec. 28th - 1919. At Dr. Kemisar's orders. Very resp't, J.M. Very truly yours, Fred C. Morgan Superintendent. SJ-Encls. 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Agency, Wespelem, Wash., Apr. 14, 1919 Supt. E. H. Hammond, Cushman School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Mr. Hammond; The mother of George Friedlander, one of your pupils from this Reservation was in the Office this morning inquiring about George's health. She tells me she hears that he is sick and in the hospital, and has a severe cough. It will be appreciated if you will advise me as soon as possible as to George's condition, in order that I may notify the mother and relieve her anxiety. Very respectfully, Fred C. Morgan, Superintendent. By Alvin Barbour Clerk. AB:AJ Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington, Apr. 24, 1919 Mr. Fred C. Morgan Colville Agency Nespelem, Wash. My dear Mr. Morgan, In reply to your letter of April 14 regarding condition of George Friedlander: George is, at present, in the hospital under observation and treatment for a bad cold. He has been given a special Diet and has been under observation for two weeks and was progressing favorably until he caught a cold. We will watch George carefully and will report to his mother his progress. From what the doctor tells me, I do not feel alarmed at George's condition. In case it does become worse, I will send him home. Very respectfully, Superintendent. EHH:MG Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington March 26, 1919. Mr. Fred C. Morgan Nespelem, Washington. My dear Mr. Morgan: I am sending your herewith the report of the physical examination given George Friedlander by Doctor Kinnear, which shows that he has lost four pounds since he entered here, due principally to the "flu". George has been placed on special diet and I feel sure that he will soon be as well and as strong as ever. He is really not sick now. Very truly yours, Superintendent EHH:Jenc Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington March 21, 1919. Mr. Fred C. Morgan Nespelem, Washington. Dear Mr. Morgan: At the time Emily wrote her mother, George Friedlander was recovering from an attack of the Grippe. However, George has been out of the hospital since the third of this month and whenever questioned concerning his health he answers "allright." I have asked Dr. Kinnear to give him a thorough examination and will see that he does so. Very sincerely yours, Superintendent EHH:T 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash., March 10, 1919. Mr. H.H. Hammond, Supt., Cushman Trades School, Cassema, Wash. Dear Mr. Hammond: The mother of George Freidlander called at my office today and informed me that she had received a letter from Emily Friedlander, her little daughter, attending your school, stating that George was in very bad health and thought he should return home. George's mother was distressed about the matter and asked me to write you about it, requesting me to ask that he should be returned home, if he is in very bad health. She desires that you personally will take the matter up and have the Doctor examine her son and write her at once regarding his health. I will appreciate your immediate attention to this matter. Please advise me as well as his mother about the matter. Very respectfully, Fred A. Morgan Superintendent. W.E.G. Humphries. DSI. Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Dec. 17, 1918. Supt. Fred C. Morgan, Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash. Dear Mr. Morgan: Replying to your letter of December 11th relative to George Friedlander's request for more funds, would say that George has a balance of $23.00 at the present time. He bought a suit of clothes for $25.00 last Saturday. His present balance is sufficient for his needs until sometime next spring before the vacation. Very respectfully, Superintendent 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash. December 11, 1918. Superintendent E. H. Hammond, Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Washington. Dear Mr. Hammond: I have received a letter from George Friedlander in which he requests that I send him $45.00. On November 13th a check in the sum of $50.00 was sent to you for his account. I am of the opinion that this amount should be sufficient for his needs until next spring. However I would appreciate your recommendation of his request. Very respectfully, Fred C. Morgan Superintendent. Sm:A George has all the money he needs. He has a balance of $23.00 on hand. He bought a suit for $5.00 last Saturday. CASE RECORD. Francis will send her children to the Cushman School and she is on her way to Okanogan to buy clothing for them and I have given her a purchase order on the account of George Freidlander for $10 and one on the account of Emily Freidlander for $5 for clothing.
